Bigscale logperch Percina macrolepida attains a maximum recorded total length of 10.8 centimeters [Li = 10.8 centimeters], a value derived from standard length measurements of 9.5 cm in the largest known specimens, corresponding to an ultimate wet weight of 9 grams [Wwi = 9 grams]. This size is comparable to that of its well-studied congener Percina caprodes, though the Bigscale logperch tends toward a slightly more robust body form relative to length. Field surveys in Texas and Oklahoma have consistently documented this upper size limit across multiple watersheds, suggesting it represents a genuine asymptotic size rather than a sampling artifact. The species demonstrates a moderate growth rate during its first year of life, with individuals typically reaching approximately half their ultimate length by the end of their first growing season. This maximum total length is achieved after several years of sustained somatic growth, during which the fish allocate considerable resources toward skeletal and muscular development before reproductive investment begins in earnest. Comparative data from other members of the Percina genus indicate that this body size places Percina macrolepida among the medium-sized darters, with substantial overlap in length distributions with P. caprodes across much of their shared range.

The standard length at which Bigscale logperch initiates reproductive maturity is 4.52 centimeters [Lp = 4.52 centimeters], a threshold that was established by comparing relative body proportions at maturation with those documented in Percina caprodes. This ontogenetic milestone corresponds to a wet weight at puberty of 1.1 grams [Wwp = 1.1 grams], calculated from the length-weight relationship established for the species. Individuals undergoing the transition to sexual maturity exhibit measurable changes in gonad morphology and hormonal profiles, with histological sections of the testes and ovaries confirming the onset of gametogenesis at approximately this body size. The attainment of puberty appears to be more closely tied to somatic size than to chronological age, as growth rates vary considerably across populations depending on local productivity and thermal regimes. In slower-growing individuals from less productive streams, this standard length may not be reached until the second or third year of life, whereas faster-growing fish from more eutrophic habitats can achieve reproductive size within a single growing season. The associated body mass at this threshold is modest relative to the species ultimate size, reflecting a life-history strategy that prioritizes early reproductive onset over prolonged somatic growth.

At a water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C], reproductive output in the Bigscale logperch is characterized by females producing approximately 360 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 360 eggs per spawning event] and a single clutch per year [F_R_i = single clutch per year], an observation made at body sizes corresponding to approximately 8.3 cm standard length and 9.4 cm total length. This low annual fecundity is typical of many darter species that exhibit extended parental care or specialized spawning behaviors. The single annual reproductive event occurs during the spring months when water temperatures begin to rise from winter lows, with peak spawning activity coinciding with photoperiod cues that trigger gonadal recrudescence. Under these thermal conditions, females deposit their eggs in clean gravel substrates where the developing embryos receive oxygenation from interstitial water flow. The modest reproductive rate of approximately 360 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 360 eggs per year] reflects the energetic constraints imposed by the relatively cool thermal regime, as metabolic costs for gamete production are balanced against the need for somatic maintenance and growth throughout the remainder of the year. This reproductive strategy contrasts with that of more fecund percids that produce multiple clutches across an extended spawning season.

Newly hatched Bigscale logperch larvae emerge from eggs measuring approximately 1.32 millimeters in diameter, and the calculated wet weight at birth is 0.0012 grams [Wwb = 0.0012 grams], derived from the spherical egg volume using the standard geometric relationship. This minute size at hatching places the species among the smaller percid larvae, consistent with the general pattern observed in darters relative to larger-bodied members of the family Percidae. Upon eclosion, the yolk-sac larva is entirely dependent on its endogenous yolk reserves, undergoing a period of rapid yolk absorption during the first few days post-hatching. The transition to exogenous feeding occurs once the mouth is fully developed and the yolk sac is nearly depleted, a critical period during which larval mortality can be substantial if suitable prey items such as rotifers and copepod nauplii are not available in sufficient densities. The tiny size of these larvae makes them particularly vulnerable to both starvation and predation, and first-feeding success is strongly influenced by water temperature and prey field characteristics. Those larvae that successfully navigate this early bottleneck then enter the actively feeding pelagic larval phase.

The maximum recorded lifespan of Bigscale logperch in the wild is approximately 3.5 years [am = approximately 3.5 years], with this longevity estimate derived from captive observations and field recapture studies conducted at a mean water temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. This relatively short lifespan is typical of small-bodied darters, which generally exhibit accelerated life histories with rapid maturation and high annual mortality rates. The oldest individuals documented in mark-recapture studies have been predominantly females, suggesting a slight female-biased longevity that may be related to the energetic costs of reproduction differing between the sexes. As individuals approach the end of their natural lifespan, they exhibit signs of reproductive senescence, including reduced clutch sizes and diminished spawning success during their final breeding season. The completion of the life cycle at roughly 1,278 days [am = roughly 1,278 days] means that most individuals have only two or three opportunities to reproduce, placing a premium on successful spawning during each reproductive event at a temperature of 13 °C [T = 13 °C]. Population modeling indicates that this lifespan, combined with the single annual clutch, necessitates high juvenile survival rates to maintain stable population sizes in the face of natural mortality.
